content: Tuberculosis of the spine, while generally treatable with chemotherapy, has raised debates regarding the necessity of surgical intervention in the small percentage of affected individuals (1-2%). This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of combining chemotherapy with surgery compared to chemotherapy alone in managing active spinal tuberculosis. To investigate this, researchers conducted a systematic search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to February 2010. A subsequent search in November 2012 did not identify any new studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a minimum follow-up period of one year, specifically comparing chemotherapy plus surgery versus chemotherapy alone for active tuberculosis of the thoracic and/or lumbar spine. Two RCTs, involving a total of 331 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These trials were conducted in the 1970s and 1980s, with follow-up data available at intervals of 18 months, three years, five years, and, in one trial, 10 years. However, follow-up completeness varied, with less than 80% of participants available for analysis at several time points. The trials assessed outcomes such as kyphosis angle, neurological deficits, bony fusion, absence of spinal tuberculosis, mortality, activity level regained, changes in allocated treatment, and bone loss. Pain was not reported in either trial. The results showed no statistically significant differences between the two treatment groups for any of the measured outcomes. Among the 130 participants who received chemotherapy alone, 12 developed neurological deficits, and five required decompression surgery. One trial suggested that an initial kyphosis angle greater than 30° was more likely to worsen, particularly in children. The authors concluded that the two trials included in this review were underpowered to determine whether routine surgery offers additional benefits. Despite advancements in medical and surgical techniques since the time of these studies, the findings do not support routine surgical intervention for spinal tuberculosis outside the context of a large, well-designed RCT. Clinicians may still consider surgery for specific patient groups based on individual clinical indications. Future research should explore these issues further, including the perspectives of patients regarding their disease and treatment.
